activities.title: Meet sh in words
materials: words: ship, shop, shut, fish, dish, wish, shell
parentPrompts: Say "shhh" like asking for quiet. Explain: "Two letters, s and h, team up to make one sound. We call that a digraph."
Write "sh" on a card. Read ship, shop, fish, dish slowly, tapping the sh as one sound (not two).
Hunt in the room for things you can name that have sh (shoe, shelf, dish, brush, fish if you have a toy).
Write two sh words together on paper and underline the sh in each.
Check: when you point to the words, your child reads sh as one sound, not "s-h." Count how many of the seven words they read correctly.

activities.title: Meet ch in words
materials: words: chip, chop, chin, chat, much, such, rich, lunch
parentPrompts: Say "chuh" like a train: ch-ch-ch. Explain that c and h team up to make one sound, the ch digraph.
Read chip, chop, chin, chat. Then read much, such, rich, lunch, where the ch comes at the end. Ask: "Where do you hear it, the beginning or the end?"
Make two piles on the table, Beginning and End. Sort the word cards.
Dictate "chop" and "much." Your child writes them, underlining the ch.
Check: your child sorts correctly and reads six of the eight words.

activities.title: Meet th and wh in words
materials: words: this, that, then, thin, math, bath, when, whip, whiz
parentPrompts: Show your child how to make the th sound: tongue gently between the teeth and blow air. Try it in a mirror. Explain that "this" has a voiced th and "thin" has a quiet, whispery th; both are written th.
Read this, that, then, thin, math, bath. Ask: "Which ones feel buzzy? Which are just air?" (Do not worry if your child cannot tell. Hearing it is enough.)
Introduce wh: say "when" and "whip." Explain that in most places wh sounds like w.
Play "digraph detective." Hold up a card and have your child say sh, ch, th, or wh before reading it.
Check: your child identifies the correct digraph on at least six cards and reads the words.

activities.title: Sort words by digraph and meet ck
materials: words: ship, chop, thin, whip, duck, sock, neck, much, fish, bath, chin, when
parentPrompts: Write the twelve words on cards. Make four labeled spots: sh, ch, th, wh. Introduce "ck" as the extra team at the end of short words like duck and sock; it makes the k sound.
Have your child sort the words into the four spots (ck words will need a fifth spot).
Read each pile aloud. Ask your child to think of one more word that fits each pile. Write it on a new card.
Pick one word from each pile and have your child write it.
Check: sorting is correct for at least ten of the twelve cards, and your child can name the digraph in each.

activities.title: Write sentences with digraph words
materials: a few word cards from this week
parentPrompts: Read three practice sentences aloud and have your child repeat each: "The fish is in the dish." "I chop the chip." "This is a thin duck."
Say the first sentence again. Count the words on your fingers. Have your child write it, spelling the digraph words with sh, ch, th, ck.
Check it together: capital letter, finger spaces, end mark. Let your child fix one thing, not everything.
Have your child write their own sentence using at least one digraph word and read it to you.
Check: digraphs are spelled correctly in most of the words and the sentence begins with a capital and ends with a mark.

subject: math
title: Teen numbers are a ten and some ones

activities.title: Build teen numbers
materials: an egg carton cut down to 10 spots (a homemade ten-frame)
parentPrompts: Fill an egg carton (10 spots) with counters. Add 4 more outside the carton. Ask: "How many in all?" Say: "A ten and four more is fourteen."
Build 12, 15, 17 and 19 with a full carton plus ones. Each time say: "ten and ___ ones makes ___."
Write the numbers 14 and 19 and point out that the 1 means one ten and the other digit is the ones.
Call out a teen number and have your child build it.
Check: your child builds three teen numbers correctly and tells you how many tens and ones each has.

activities.title: Fill the ten, then add the rest
materials: a ten-frame drawn on paper (two rows of five)
parentPrompts: Put 8 counters in the ten-frame. Add 5 more in a different color. Ask: "How can we make a full ten first?" Move 2 into the frame.
Say: "8 + 5 is the same as 8 + 2 + 3. That is 10 + 3 = 13." Write it.
Try 9 + 4 (move 1 to make ten), 7 + 6, and 8 + 7.
Ask: "Which number needs fewer to make ten?" and let your child choose which to fill.
Check: your child fills the ten-frame first and gets the right total on at least two of four problems, explaining the steps.

activities.title: Add to 20 with games
materials: 2 dice or number cards from 1 to 9
parentPrompts: Roll two dice and write the numbers. For sums over 10, make a ten first with counters or the ten-frame.
Play "beat the total": each player rolls twice and adds, and the higher total wins a point. Play to five points.
Pick one round and ask: "How did you add it? Did you count on, use a double, or make a ten?" There are many good strategies.
Write three of the equations from the game.
Check: your child adds sums up to 20 with a strategy and can explain one of them. Do not expect fluency yet; strategy talk is the goal.

activities.title: Add three groups
materials: 12 small objects in three different colors or kinds
parentPrompts: Show 3 red, 4 blue, and 2 green blocks. Ask: "How many in all?" Look for two numbers that are easy to add first (3 + 4 = 7, then 7 + 2 = 9).
Try the numbers in another order. Ask: "Do we get the same total if we add 4 + 2 first?"
Solve a story: "Mia saw 5 birds, 3 squirrels and 2 rabbits. How many animals in all?" Look for pairs that make ten when you can.
Let your child make up an adding-three problem for you.
Check: your child solves two three-number problems (total 20 or less) and knows the order of adding does not change the total.

activities.title: Subtract using ten
parentPrompts: Put 13 counters out (a full ten-frame and 3 extra). Ask: "Take away 4. How can the ten help?" Take the 3 extras first, then 1 from the ten.
Write 13 - 4 = 9 and say it. Show it again as "13 - 3 = 10, and 10 - 1 = 9."
Try 12 - 5, 15 - 7, and 14 - 6. Let your child choose how to take away.
Write the matching addition fact for one: 9 + 4 = 13.
Check: your child solves at least three of four and explains one strategy with the ten-frame.

activities.title: Match animal parts to jobs
materials: picture books or printed pictures of animals (a bird, a fish, a rabbit, a turtle)
parentPrompts: Look at an animal picture. Ask: "What parts do you see? What might each one help the animal do?" (Wings and feathers help birds fly; fins help fish swim.)
Look at a bird beak and a duck foot. Ask: "How do you think the webbed foot helps a duck?" (It pushes water when swimming.)
Fold paper into four boxes. Draw four animals and one body part for each, then say what the part does.
Play "I am a part": say "I help a fish move through water" (fin).
Check: your child names at least three animal parts and a true job for each.

activities.title: Compare animal coverings
materials: pictures or toys of a rabbit, a duck, a turtle, and a fish
a feather and a cotton ball (optional)
parentPrompts: Show each animal covering. Ask: "How might fur, feathers, or scales help this animal?"
Try it: dip a feather in water and shake. Dip a paper towel in water. Ask: "Which one stays dry? How might that help a duck?" Many feathers shed water better than paper does.
Talk about a turtle shell. Ask: "How might a shell help a turtle stay safe?"
Sort pictures of animals by what covers them: fur, feathers, scales, shell.
Check: your child sorts animals by covering and says how one covering helps the animal. Safety: wash hands after handling any feather, and do not pick up feathers or touch wild animals outdoors.

activities.title: Test tools like beaks
materials: rice, water in a shallow dish, small pebbles
parentPrompts: Explain: birds have different beaks for different jobs. Show pictures of a hummingbird, a duck, and an eagle if you have them.
Pretend your tools are beaks. Use tweezers to pick up rice from a plate (like a small bird picking seeds). Use a spoon to scoop water (like a duck). Use a clothespin to grab a pebble.
Ask: "Which tool was best for which job? Which was hard?"
Draw your favorite bird with its beak and write what the beak does.
Check: your child connects a tool to a job and says one reason the tool fits the job.

activities.title: Learn about community helpers
materials: a library book or pictures about community helpers
parentPrompts: Look at pictures of helpers: a firefighter, a nurse, a mail carrier, a librarian, a bus driver, a teacher. Ask: "What does each person do? How do they help?"
Ask: "Which helpers have you seen near your home?"
Have your child draw one helper and write a sentence: "A mail carrier brings letters."
Play charades. Act out a job and have the others guess.
Check: your child names four helpers and tells what they do. Remind your child that many different people can do any of these jobs.

activities.title: Ask good questions
materials: a helper to talk to (a family member, a neighbor, or a worker at a library or store), in person or by phone
parentPrompts: Pick a helper your child knows or someone you can call. Explain: "An interview is when you ask someone questions to learn about their job."
Together, make three questions: "What do you do each day? What tools do you use? What do you like about your job?"
Hold the interview. Your child asks the questions and writes or draws what they learn.
After, ask: "What did you learn that surprised you?"
Check: your child asks all the questions and retells one thing they learned. If you cannot arrange a real interview, play pretend with a toy helper.
